title: Maryland started the battery race. We shouldn’t cede the lead now
summary: Maryland was at the forefront of the call for energy storage, which stabilizes costs and improves reliability, writes Diane Cherry, but other states have now surpassed the state's goals and Maryland cannot afford to let storage drift off the agenda.
content:
by Diane Cherry, Maryland Matters June 17, 2026

by Diane Cherry, Maryland Matters June 17, 2026

Maryland electricity prices have surged due to compounding factors: data center construction, the electrification of buildings and transportation, and geopolitical uncertainty. With summer approaching, homeowners will only see higher bills as air conditioners get turned on across the state. More batteries can help.

Electricity costs spike during peak usage times — when everyone does laundry, charges their EVs, and blasts the AC. These activities drive prices higher than almost anything else. When demand spikes, so does pricing and consumers and businesses bear that cost.

As most followers of the State House know, Maryland’s Utility RELIEF Act, signed into law this spring, aims to save typical households at least $150 a year on energy bills. It introduces stricter regulations on utility companies, advanced grid-enhancing technologies, and data center energy demands.

Less well known is how the RELIEF Act also advances Maryland’s energy storage procurement program. It frames energy storage as a reliability resource. It clarifies the Public Service Commission’s authority, contract structure, and performance expectations for transmission-connected storage projects.

Maryland’s legislative session ended in mid-April, but the real work now falls to the PSC: Finishing what it started on the state’s 3-gigawatt battery energy storage target, to help stabilize electricity prices for residents already stretched thin.

Batteries store cheaper, off-peak power and discharge it during high-demand periods, reducing the need for expensive “peaker” plants and easing strain on the grid. This lowers wholesale prices and, ultimately, the costs passed on to ratepayers.

Other states have already begun addressing high electricity prices with energy storage. According to a recent report by Wood Mackenzie, the U.S. hit a record 18.9 GW of battery storage installations in 2025 — enough to power 13.5 million households — with growth expanding into states beyond the traditional leaders of California and Texas, such as New Jersey and Virginia.

Maryland has already laid the groundwork to join the wave. The state set a 3 GW storage target in 2023 and directed the PSC to develop an implementation program to meet it within 10 years.

Then, Gov. Wes Moore signed the Next Generation Energy Act in 2023, instructing the PSC to issue bids for 1.6 GW of storage in two rounds of 800 megawatts each. It also required investor-owned electric utilities in the state to collectively build or buy at least 150 MW of distribution-connected, front-of-the-meter energy storage.

Bids for the first 800 MW went out in January, with awards expected in October. The second 800 MW tranche is slated to launch next January. County-level zoning updates show the infrastructure falling into place.

What Maryland cannot afford: letting the over 1,000 MW remaining of its 3 GW target drift off the agenda.

Other states in the region have now surpassed Maryland’s goals. Storage has become an economic and ratepayer issue, not just an environmental one — and Maryland’s neighbors have started treating it that way.

New Jersey’s new governor, on her first day in office, signed executive orders declaring a utility affordability emergency and calling for expanded deployment of solar and battery storage.

Virginia passed bills through both chambers this session to dramatically expand its energy storage mandate — setting a new target of 20 GW, which would make it the largest utility-scale storage procurement of any state in the PJM Interconnection, the regional grid operator for the Mid-Atlantic.

Storage goes beyond economic opportunity; it stabilizes homeowners’ and businesses’ energy bills on an increasingly volatile grid.

Marylanders who lost power during the winter freeze earlier this year know what it costs when the grid has no buffer. As extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, conversations about grid resilience have moved from the control room to the kitchen table.

Another feature of this year’s Utility RELIEF Act would redirect $100 million previously collected from ratepayers toward auctions for solar energy generation projects, plus co-located or stand-alone battery storage facilities across the state.

The PSC’s procurement work demonstrates the regulatory appetite. As the legislative session ends, implementation takes center stage.

Maryland has spent years building toward this. Energy storage stabilizes costs for families already stretched thin. The Utility RELIEF Act marked the next step. But passing it means nothing if Maryland lets the rest of its 3 GW goal stall. The PSC has the authority to maintain that momentum, and it should make every effort to do so in January, when the next period of project submissions opens.
